_comment: Gates whose failure is KNOWN, JUSTIFIED and deliberately carried past the
push guard. This is not a way to push green CI -- CI still runs every gate
and still fails on anything listed here. It only lets the push HAPPEN, with
the failure named on the record instead of routed around silently.
block-unverified-push.sh enforces three things, and the last two are what
stop this becoming a permanent allowlist:
1. every FAILING gate must appear here, or the push is still refused;
2. every gate here must actually be failing -- a stale entry REFUSES,
so an excuse cannot outlive the failure it excuses;
3. the reason must be substantive, the same bar .dead-bash-allowlist
applies and gate-test:dead-bash proves with a low-effort-BLOCKER case.
A narrowed run (--only/--skip) is refused before any of this is consulted,
so carrying cannot become a second way to launder a partial lane.

carried.reason: REASON REWRITTEN 2026-09-14, because the previous one was refuted by running it. It said the only cure was `--refresh`, that this needs an admin:org token, that no assistant session has one, and that the fix was therefore door:operator-only. `--refresh` was run from an ordinary session and SUCCEEDED: 'refreshed 3 reference(s) across 3 repo(s)', and it correctly recorded that renet can read BWS_ACCESS_TOKEN (via=repo). The stale-record half of the old reason is gone. What remains is the real and narrower blocker: console workflows reference `secrets.BREAKPOINT_TUNNEL_TOKEN`, which that repository CANNOT read (via=absent) because the org secrets were deleted 2026-09-05. No refresh can fix that -- the value does not exist anywhere to be reached -- and the two cures, minting the secret or deleting the reference from breakpoint.yml, are both operator decisions about a live debugging surface. door:operator-only, on the NEW evidence rather than the old. Carried, not suppressed: CI still runs this gate and still fails on it, and this entry goes stale and REFUSES the moment the reference resolves.

A LOCAL MEASUREMENT ARTIFACT, and the gate's own comment describes this exact failure mode: 'a full run that overlapped two other sessions on 2026-09-02 pushed a 4.5s gate's average to 21s and this oracle demanded it be marked slow'. The three gates it names here (check:ci-guard-mention-anchoring 24.8s, check:ci-changed-selection 141.6s, gate-test:policy-liveness-floors 29.2s) were timed on a machine that spent today running a 22-worker gate battery and a 15919-test pytest suite, so the numbers are inflated by my own load. The oracle reads .ci/cache/gate-durations.json, which .gitignore:143 excludes, so CI's checkout does not have this file and the read sits inside a try/except -- these findings cannot reproduce there. Marking three gates `slow: true` on a contended measurement would change CI lane composition on bad data, which is the one thing the gate's comment warns against. Carried so CI can measure it honestly and say so.

zot is pinned 2.1.20 and upstream has 2.1.21. REAL, not environmental, and it will be red in CI too -- CI has a token, and this gate can only see upstream when the GitHub API is not rate-limiting it. I tried to land it and stopped deliberately: private/renet/Dockerfile pins a SHA256 PER ARCHITECTURE (ZOT_SHA256_AMD64 and ZOT_SHA256_ARM64) and verifies them with `sha256sum -c -` at build time. The arm64 artifact downloaded and hashes to 49e1f948af8e5c6ed5c803bad4508cf7af37be6c15b7fb2840109900b916eb48; the amd64 artifact returned HTTP 504 on every one of seven attempts across three retry rounds. Bumping the version with only one verified hash would fail the image build at the checksum step for every amd64 consumer, which is strictly worse than staying a release behind. The bump is a five-minute job the moment that URL answers. Carried rather than blocklisted, because this is a transient upstream outage and not a decision to hold zot back.
